children.text: What Is Play? How Does Play Happen?

From childhood make-believe and theatre to sports and market speculation, play takes many forms. It can entertain and offer a break from everyday routines. It can also give us a way to explore possibilities: we try out roles, test limits, follow rules, bend them, or imagine a different world for a while.

We play with real objects and abstract ideas, with friends, loved ones, and strangers. We play alone, together, and sometimes across species. Play is often described as practice—a way to develop physical skills, learn social cues, or meet the unexpected in a relatively safe setting. These ideas offer a functionalist understandings of play. However they do little in showing us, how does play actually happen?
The ambiguity of play

“Play” is a useful idea partly because it is hard to pin down. No single activity is always play. Chasing can be a game, a hunt, or an attempt to escape. Wrestling can be play or a serious fight. Many of us have had the experience where we genuinely find a friendly tease that can be an insult otherwise funny. The same action can mean different things depending on who is doing it, what came before, and how the other participants respond.
Biologist and anthropologist Gregory Bateson offers a way to think about this uncertainty

. Watching monkeys play, he noticed that a playful nip could resemble a real bite in every way, yet participants of play would "just know". What made it different was signals -- often subtle ones -- that the action belonged to another kind of interaction. Bateson described this as a message about the message: in effect, “This is play.” The participants were not only acting; they were helping frame how their actions should be understood. That frame is not always announced in a clear or separate signal. It can emerge through timing, repetition, gesture, sound, and response. One participant makes an invitation; another accepts, ignores, or changes it. The play continues as the participants adjust to each other. In this sense, play is not just a thing an individual does. It is something participants make together.

children.text: Looking at play through a multi-species lens
The scientific study of animal play dates back over a century. Psychologist Karl Groos's book
The Play of Animals

(Groos, 1898) proposed that play serves a developmental and evolutionary function rather than being mere frivolity. For much of the twentieth century, though, play was treated as a marginal topic, too hard to define and too easily anthropomorphized for serious study. That began to change in the 1960s and 70s, when field primatologists like Jane Goodall, observing wild chimpanzees at Gombe, documented play-panting, tickling, and social play in rich naturalistic detail, l suggesting deep continuities between animal and human behavior.
The Genesis of Animal Play: Testing the Limits
, set a five formal criteria of play, meant to let researchers decide, rigorously, whether a given behavior counts as play rather than just being labeled that loosely:
The behavior is not fully functional in the context in which it appears — it doesn’t contribute directly to survival in that moment (e.g., play-fighting isn’t real fighting).
It’s spontaneous, voluntary, intentional, pleasurable, or otherwise rewarding to the animal, rather than forced.
It’s structurally or temporally different from the “serious” version of the behavior — incomplete, exaggerated, awkward, or occurring earlier in life than the functional version would (precocious).
It’s repeated, but not in a rigid, identical way each time — there’s variation.
It happens when the animal is relaxed, healthy, well-fed, and not under stress — “surplus resource” conditions, not survival pressure.

Overall, play is widespread among mammals, but it does not look the same everywhere. A young animal may chase, tumble, or spar with a companion; another may manipulate an object or repeat a movement alone. Researchers study play in many species to ask what it makes possible: practice, learning, flexibility, social connection, or simply an enjoyable activity in the present. There may be no single answer that applies to every animal or every kind of play.
Why do we talk about play?
A provocation of interconnectedness

It is only recently that we have come to see animals as creatures of sentience and feeling, kin to us in ways Descartes could not allow when he cast them as unfeeling machines, mere automata without "soul" as inner life.

Against that long shadow, researchers have only in the last few decades begun to document play across the animal world, and expanding the framework of play to more species. For instance, play was long assumed absent in reptiles until Gordon Burghardt’s studies of a turtle batting a ball, and later of monitor lizards and crocodiles, challenged that.
Deciding who plays is an act of category-making, a drawing and redrawing of boundaries that says as much about our own assumptions as about the animals we study.

What, then, do we gain by treating play as an analytical category at all? Following Gregory Bateson’s sense of ecology as a web of relations rather than a collection of separate parts, this project holds that play offers a way of thinking planetary interconnectedness from the ground up: a form of contact that is neither purely functional nor purely frivolous, through which lives remain bound to one another without ever collapsing into sameness. Inspired by past research on play in both humans and animals, this project brings a particular, under-examined mode of play into closer view, asking, provocatively, what play makes possible between lives that are connected yet never quite the same. What happens if we think of the essence of sentience and consiousness as playfulness rather than critical reason and intelligence?
